paras.text: Organic compounds absorb energy on interaction with electromagnetic radiations. The electromagnetic radiation (emr) extends from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. X–rays and gamma rays (very high energy) are so energetic that they excite electrons, above all the energy levels, causing ionization. Energies in the ultraviolet–visible range excite electrons to higher energy levels within molecules. Infrared energies excite molecular vibrations, and microwave energies excite rotations. Radio-wave frequencies (very low energy) excite the nuclear spin transitions observed in NMR spectroscopy. Unlike chemical tests (classical methods of analysis), most of the spectroscopic and chromatographic techniques are nondestructive, required small amount of sample, less time consuming and provide more accurate and rapid results. These methods are simple and do not involve much chemistry as compared to the classical methods. The regions of electromagnetic spectrum of electromagnetic radiations are given in Figure 24.2.

24.2 Modern Methods of Analysis

مادے کے ساتھ برقی مقناطیسی شعاعوں کے تعامل کو سپیکٹروسکوپی کہتے ہیں۔ سپیکٹروسکوپی کسی مرکب کی طرف سے جذب (یا خارج) ہونے والی روشنی کی مقدار کی روشنی کی طولِ موج (یا تعدد) کے تفاعل کے طور پر پیمائش ہے۔ عموماً سپیکٹرومیٹر نمونے پر روشنی ڈالتا ہے، گزرنے والی روشنی کی مقدار کو طولِ موج (یا تعدد) کے تفاعل کے طور پر ناپتا ہے اور نتائج کو گراف پر بناتا ہے جسے طیف کہتے ہیں۔

نامیاتی مرکبات برقی مقناطیسی شعاعوں سے تعامل پر توانائی جذب کرتے ہیں۔ برقی مقناطیسی شعاعیں (emr) زیادہ توانائی والی گاما شعاعوں سے کم توانائی والی ریڈیائی لہروں تک پھیلی ہوئی ہیں۔ ایکس ریز اور گاما شعاعیں (بہت زیادہ توانائی) اتنی توانا ہیں کہ یہ الیکٹرانوں کو تمام توانائی سطحوں سے اوپر ابھار کر آئنائزیشن پیدا کرتی ہیں۔ بالائے بنفشی–مرئی حد کی توانائیاں سالمات کے اندر الیکٹرانوں کو اونچی توانائی سطحوں تک ابھارتی ہیں۔ زیریں سرخ توانائیاں سالماتی ارتعاشات اور مائیکرو ویو توانائیاں گردش کو ابھارتی ہیں۔ ریڈیائی لہروں کے تعدد (بہت کم توانائی) NMR سپیکٹروسکوپی میں مشاہدہ ہونے والی مرکزی سپن کی منتقلیوں کو ابھارتے ہیں۔ کیمیائی ٹیسٹوں (تجزیے کے روایتی طریقوں) کے برعکس زیادہ تر سپیکٹروسکوپی اور کرومیٹوگرافی تکنیکیں نمونے کو تباہ نہیں کرتیں، کم نمونہ درکار ہوتا ہے، کم وقت لیتی ہیں اور زیادہ درست اور تیز نتائج دیتی ہیں۔ یہ طریقے سادہ ہیں اور روایتی طریقوں کے مقابلے میں ان میں زیادہ کیمیا شامل نہیں۔ برقی مقناطیسی شعاعوں کے طیف کے خطے شکل 24.2 میں دیے گئے ہیں۔

Practice problem 12.1

Vanillin, a flavoring agent, is made up of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. When a sample of vanillin weighing 2.50 g burns in oxygen, 5.79 g of carbon dioxide and 1.188 g of water are obtained. The molecular mass of vanillin determined from mass spectrometry is 152.15 amu. Calculate the empirical and molecular formulae of vanillin.

Glucose has C = 39.99%, H = 6.72% and O = 53.2%. Molecular mass of glucose is 180 amu: Calculate its empirical and molecular formulae.

24.2 Modern Methods of Analysis

Structural identification is of prime importance in organic chemistry, as it provides complete information about that substance. The molecular formula of organic compound determined from combustion analysis may not give complete information about structure, as a number of structures (isomers) may be possible for the given formula. When a compound is isolated from a natural source or synthesized, its structure must be completely determined prior to applications.

In many cases, a compound can be identified by chemical means. We find the molecular formula by analyzing the elemental composition and determining the molecular weight. If the compound has been characterized before, we can compare its physical properties (melting point, boiling point, etc.) with the published values. For example; C₂H₆O is the molecular formula of both ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether. But ethyl alcohol (C₂H₅OH) at room temperature is liquid and its boiling point is 78°C, while dimethyl ether (CH₃—O—CH₃) is gas at room temperature having a boiling point of –24°C. Chemical tests can suggest the functional groups and narrow the range of possible structures before the physical properties are used to make an identification. For example ethanol reacts with sodium metal liberating hydrogen, while dimethyl ether does not react with it.

Chemical analysis is insufficient for new compounds that have never been synthesized and characterized. They are also impractical with compounds that are difficult to obtain, because a relatively large sample is required to complete the elemental analysis and all the functional group tests. We need analytical techniques that work with tiny samples and that do not destroy the sample. Spectroscopic techniques are modern methods of analysis which often meet these requirements.

24.2.1 Spectroscopy

The interaction of electromagnet radiations with matter is called spectroscopy. Spectroscopy is the measurement of the amount of light absorbed (or emitted) by a compound as a function of the wavelength (or frequency) of light. In general, a spectrometer irradiates the sample with light, measures the amount of light transmitted as a function of wavelength (or frequency) and plots the results on a graph, called a spectrum.

Organic compounds absorb energy on interaction with electromagnetic radiations. The electromagnetic radiation (emr) extends from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. X–rays and gamma rays (very high energy) are so energetic that they excite electrons, above all the energy levels, causing ionization. Energies in the ultraviolet–visible range excite electrons to higher energy levels within molecules. Infrared energies excite molecular vibrations, and microwave energies excite rotations. Radio-wave frequencies (very low energy) excite the nuclear spin transitions observed in NMR spectroscopy. Unlike chemical tests (classical methods of analysis), most of the spectroscopic and chromatographic techniques are nondestructive, required small amount of sample, less time consuming and provide more accurate and rapid results. These methods are simple and do not involve much chemistry as compared to the classical methods. The regions of electromagnetic spectrum of electromagnetic radiations are given in Figure 24.2.
